Lessons.Title: Base-ten Blocks to Divide
ExplanationParagraphs:
Learning goal: You will make sense of base-ten representations for division.
In the previous lesson, you applied your understanding from grade 3 to divide two- and three-digit numbers by one-digit divisors. You worked with dividends slightly beyond 100 and represented your thinking in a way that made sense to them. In this lesson, you work with larger dividends and represent problems with base-ten blocks.

Source sequence (2021): Warm-up What Do You Know About Base-ten Blocks?; Activity 1 Blocks to Divide (25 minutes); Activity 2 Show Us Your Blocks (10 minutes). Students work with physical blocks, then explain by a sketch or equations.
Place-value exchange: one hundred can be represented by ten tens, and one ten by ten ones. When there are fewer hundreds or tens than groups, exchange them before sharing.
Original activity answers: 488 ÷ 4 = 122; 104 ÷ 8 = 13; 96 ÷ 4 = 24; 86 ÷ 2 = 43; 108 ÷ 9 = 12. A correct numeric answer alone does not prove the block model.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: show base-ten exchanges for 132 ÷ 6. Regroup 1 hundred to 10 tens, share 12 of 13 tens, regroup the leftover ten into ones and share 12 ones: result 22; check 6×22=132.
Source teacher-only review: grade physical construction, notes, diagrams and group display independently. Publisher-original protected Cool-down and image are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Division as equal sharing of place-value units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Dividing the total among equal groups gives one equal quantity per group.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Build dividend from hundreds, tens and ones, then share each unit value across the divisor groups.
KeyConcepts.Example: 488=4 hundreds+8 tens+8 ones; share among 4 groups to obtain 122.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exchange larger units without changing the number
KeyConcepts.Definition: One hundred equals ten tens; one ten equals ten ones.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If a place-value unit cannot be distributed, trade that unit into ten of the next smaller unit before sharing.
KeyConcepts.Example: 104÷8: exchange the hundred for ten tens; each group first gets one ten.

KeyConcepts.Title: Verify the complete equal groups
KeyConcepts.Definition: The groups must have equal values and account for every unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply the quotient by the divisor to verify the original dividend and explain each exchange.
KeyConcepts.Example: 108÷9=12, because 9×12=108 after exchanging a hundred into tens.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 1: 488 ÷ 4 without exchange
WorkedExamples.Question: Use base-ten blocks to divide 488 among four equal groups.
WorkedExamples.Method: Distribute the hundreds, tens, and ones directly.
Steps: Make 4 hundred blocks, 8 ten blocks and 8 one blocks.
Give each of four groups one hundred, two tens and two ones.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 1: 104 ÷ 8 with exchanges
WorkedExamples.Question: Use base-ten blocks to share 104 among eight equal groups.
WorkedExamples.Method: Trade the hundred into ten tens; trade the remaining two tens into ones.
Steps: Represent 104 as 1 hundred and 4 ones. Exchange the hundred for 10 tens.
Give one ten to each of eight groups; 2 tens remain. Trade 2 tens for 20 ones and add the 4 existing ones.
Share 24 ones equally among eight groups, three each; each group has 10+3=13.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 2: blocks, sketches and all three quotients
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve and model each: 96 ÷ 4, 86 ÷ 2 and 108 ÷ 9.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use equal groups with a place-value exchange when needed.
Steps: 96÷4: distribute eight tens as 2 tens per group; exchange the remaining ten for 10 ones, join the 6 ones and share 16 ones as 4 per group. Result 24.
86÷2: distribute 8 tens into two groups as 4 tens each; distribute 6 ones as 3 each. Result 43.
108÷9: exchange 1 hundred for 10 tens; share 9 tens into nine groups. Exchange remaining ten for 10 ones; add 8 ones and share 18 ones as 2 per group. Result 12.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a hundred as one unit when sharing among eight groups.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One hundred block cannot be placed intact in eight equal groups.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Exchange one hundred for ten tens, then share tens and exchange leftovers.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Leaving tens unshared because the tens count is not divisible by the group count.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Remaining tens can be exchanged for ones, preserving the total.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Exchange each remaining ten into ten ones; then finish dividing equally.

SummaryPoints: 2021 original activity numbers and place-value regrouping are represented accurately.
Explain the model (hundreds/tens/ones exchanges), not only the quotient.
A teacher checks actual blocks, drawings, oral group explanation and synthesis.
